I simulated a chain of 6 spins with the Heisenberg model H = J sum (SxSx + SySy + SzSz), with J = 1. The chain started in the perfect pattern up, down, up, down, up, down. I measured it at 6 times: 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. Each time point is one circuit. The circuits step the chain forward in steps of 0.4 (Trotter steps), so the t = 2.0 circuit has 5 steps. I sent all 6 circuits as one job to IQM's free Garnet test device (garnet:mock) with 1000 shots each. The job ID is 01a160a3-ca47-7712-9c5d-da4dfda8e54c, and it completed. It cost 0 credits.

The Neel order measures how close the chain is to the perfect alternating pattern. A value of 1 means perfect alternation. A value of 0 means no alternating pattern is left.

A perfect quantum computer running these exact circuits would show 1.00, 0.88, 0.63, 0.41, 0.35 and 0.38 at times 0 through 2.0. I got these numbers by simulating the circuits the server received, with no noise. They agree with the exact answer of the model to within 0.01 (1.00, 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.34, 0.37). The order drops quickly at first and then levels off near 0.35 to 0.4 with a small wobble.

The test device returned -0.22, -0.43, -0.42, -0.41, -0.40 and -0.42. These numbers carry no physics. The mock device does not run the circuit. It returns made-up results, here 4 fixed bit patterns in roughly equal amounts, even at t = 0 where the true answer is exactly 1. The mock is useful to check that the job is valid and runs. It cannot show the effect. To see real data you would run the same job on real Garnet, which costs credits. Real hardware would also add noise, and the deepest circuit has 73 two-qubit (CZ) gates.

The principle is this. The up-down pattern is what you would draw for classical magnets, but it is not a stable state of the quantum Heisenberg chain. The SxSx + SySy part of the energy lets each pair of neighbors swap their spins, an up-down pair becomes down-up. Those swaps spread through the chain and blur the pattern. The order does not fall back to 1. It settles at a lower value because the starting state is a mix of many quantum states.

For KCuF3, this means the copper spins do not freeze into a fixed up-down pattern, even though neighbors prefer to point opposite ways. Quantum swapping keeps the order partial and constantly shifting. Neutron scattering on KCuF3 shows the sign of this. Instead of sharp spin waves it shows a broad spread of excitations (spinons), which is what this chain model predicts. KCuF3 does order at about 39 K, but only because weak couplings between chains hold the pattern in place. A 6-spin chain is far smaller than a real crystal, so these numbers show the trend, not exact values for the material.
